title: AxiomForge LLM portability and hosting options discovery
summary: Initial migration/discovery call. AxiomForge is evaluating options to exit a mixed vendor stack (OpenAI + self-hosted vLLM) and wants parity on quality, cost, and logging for compliance. Primary concerns: private deployment options, KMS/HSM, SSO/SAML, audit logs, latency targets for chat product. Agreed to run a lightweight benchmark using a representative prompt set; Redwood will share pricing benchmarks and security whitepaper.
topics: compatibility with vLLM/TGI models and tokenization
security/compliance: SOC2, KMS, SSO, audit logs
next steps for pilot and pricing

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-01-17 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rajiv Patel (Redwood SE), Noah Li (Redwood SE observing), Lina Gomez (VP Product, AxiomForge), Daniel Ortiz (Head of ML Infra), Priya Shah (Security), Tom Everett (CTO)

Summary (auto): initial discovery to understand AxiomForge's multi-vendor exit and hosting requirements; security and eval parity emphasized; pilot and benchmark agreed.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intros, i'm maya with redwood, rajiv is our se, and we'll be leading the technical bits.
[00:08] Lina Gomez: thanks. lina here, vp product at axiomforge, we own the chat product. we're trying to consolidate vendors and get more predictable unit costs.
[00:14] Daniel Ortiz: dan here. we run a hybrid setup right now - OpenAI for most opt-in traffic, and then a vLLM cluster for specialized prompts.
[00:22] Priya Shah: priya from security, i'll be looking at compliance and encryption requirements.
[00:26] Tom Everett: tom, cto, i may hop in and out.
[00:29] Rajiv Patel: great. quick agenda: current stack & pain points, hosting modes (hosted, dedicated, private), compatibility concerns (vllm/tgi, tokenization), security/compliance checklist, pilot/benchmark next steps. sound good?
[00:41] Lina: yep. we want to make sure any migration preserves response quality — call it eval parity — and keeps latency for our chat under 250ms p50 ideally, p95 under 600ms. also cost, of course.
[00:55] Daniel: to add, our vLLM cluster gives us low-latency for context-heavy prompts but ops overhead is high and kv cache warmups are tricky.
[01:06] Maya: that matches what we hear. can you describe traffic profile quickly? rps, seq lengths?
[01:12] Daniel: baseline 80 rps for the chat product, spikes to ~320 rps on peak. seq length average 150 tokens, some long tails to 1,200 tokens for doc-summarization flows. KV cache hit rate variable, often low after deploys.
[01:27] Rajiv: good detail. sounds like batching and prefix caching will help cut unit cost, but you need careful warmup to preserve latency SLOs. on hosting modes: our hosted api is easiest to start, dedicated gives reserved gpu pools and predictable throughput, private brings your own vpc/on-prem for compliance.
[01:47] Priya: on private: we need KMS integration (customer-managed keys), audit logs with retention of 12 months, SAML/SSO and role-based access controls. also, does redwood support HSM-backed keys?
[01:58] Rajiv: yes, we integrate with most major KMS providers and support HSM-backed keys for private deployments; we can show you the architecture note. audit logs are configurable and can stream to your SIEM.
[02:09] Priya: ok good, and for data residency we may need EU-only hosting for a subset of traffic.
[02:14] Maya: we can route by region and pin specific models or routes to regions; routing policy is flexible.
[02:20] Lina: on model compatibility: we use a mix of GPT-style models via OpenAI and a couple of in-house finetunes running on vLLM/TGI. how close is the mapping? will tokenization or output differ?
[02:33] Rajiv: short answer: depends. many open models follow similar tokenization but finetunes and decoding hyperparams can cause differences. we do model onboarding where we evaluate eval parity with your prompt sets. we can run MMLU-style and custom prompt collections to measure quality drift.
[02:48] Daniel: specifically, our ops team has tuned kv cache sharding with vLLM to keep latency low on long-context prompts. does redwood preserve kv cache semantics?
[02:58] Rajiv: our runtime exposes KV cache and supports continuous caching. when moving from vLLM you'll want to compare cache hit behavior and how we handle cache warming. sometimes customers see a warmup effect on the first few minutes after deploys, but we have strategies (prefetch, persistent caches) to mitigate.
[03:16] Tom Everett: any risk of model weight or tokenization mismatches breaking scoring or hallucination profiles?
[03:23] Maya: we surface model variant mappings and can pin specific model versions. if you need exact parity with a managed OpenAI model, we can compare outputs and, if necessary, run a regression test suite. many customers find parity within acceptable tolerances after small prompt tweaks.
[03:38] Lina: whats the migration path and timeline? we prefer a pilot that runs 2-3 weeks with live canary traffic.
[03:45] Maya: works. typical pilot: start with hosted to validate parity and perf (1-2 weeks), then move to dedicated if you want reserved capacity, and private if you need full control/KMS. pilot pricing generally covers the benchmark run.
[03:58] Daniel: can we run latency benchmarks against our current vLLM setup? like you deploy a compat container and we replay traffic?
[04:06] Rajiv: yes — we can set up an eval harness. preferred approach: you share prompts + examples and a small request load, we run both quality and performance runs — include long-context cases. for throughput we can run synthetic rps to simulate spikes.
[04:21] Priya: security question: how are logs handled for hosted? does redwood see PII in logs; are transcripts stored, and for how long?
[04:30] Rajiv: by default, hosted retains logs for X days (we'll confirm exact retention in the security doc). you can opt out of retention or send logs to your S3 or SIEM; for private deployments data never leaves your VPC unless you configure otherwise. we support redaction pipelines.
[04:47] Lina: what's the SLA on latency for dedicated? and what's the fall-back behavior if a node is saturated?
[04:53] Maya: dedicated comes with throughput guarantees and an SLA; we also have smart routing and fallback to smaller model variants or other regions, configurable with automatic fallback policies to avoid errors.
[05:05] Daniel: curious about cost delta — how big is the unit cost improvement moving to dedicated vs hosted?
[05:11] Maya: it depends on utilization, batching, and quantization. in our experience, heavy-duty customers see 20-45% unit cost reductions on dedicated with optimized batching and caching; we'll share a modeled example for your workload once we see your RPS/seq-length distribution.
[05:28] Lina: can redwood host our finetunes or do we need to re-finetune on your infra?
[05:33] Rajiv: we can host model artifacts; we support common formats (hf, ggml flavors in some special cases). for finetunes, we typically validate the artifact in onboarding. sometimes tokenizers need adjustments and we help with that.
[05:46] Tom Everett: any customers who've moved off openai + vLLM mix and kept eval parity? anecdotes please.
[05:52] Maya: yes — a mid-market company in fintech moved from a hybrid setup, we ran a 2-week pilot, they hit parity on quality after prompt tuning and used dedicated for predictable throughput. they now use private for PCI-scope workloads.
[06:07] Daniel: ok good. can you comment on tooling for cost visibility? we need token-level breakdowns and tracing.
[06:13] Rajiv: redwood console provides per-route and per-model token costs, latency breakdowns, traces, and rollout controls. you can also export metrics to prometheus or datadog.
[06:25] Priya: on compliance again — do you have SOC2 Type II and ISO certifications? and do you provide penetration test reports?
[06:32] Maya: we are SOC2 compliant and have ISO controls documented; we can share the attestation and a redacted penetration test summary under NDA.
[06:41] Lina: for the eval parity tests, we want both automated scoring (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity) and human evaluation on critical flows. can you accommodate human-in-the-loop scoring?
[06:54] Rajiv: absolutely. our eval pipeline supports automated metrics and human review; we can run A/B tests and surface diffs. we'll pair with your product team for rubric definition.
[07:05] Daniel: about vLLM: some of our infra hooks depend on custom TGI endpoints; do you support TGI-compatible endpoints or adapters?
[07:13] Rajiv: we provide adapter layers and compatibility modes. many customers run a small shim to keep existing infra unchanged; we can provide example adapters for TGI/vLLM APIs.
[07:24] Maya: action items and next steps: we'll send pricing, security docs, and proposed pilot plan. dan, please share the eval prompt set and latency histograms; priya, list must-have compliance controls.
[07:34] Lina: sounds good. can we also get a sample model mapping doc — like which open model variants you'd recommend for our workloads?
[07:40] Rajiv: yes we'll include recommended variants and quantization profiles from our optimize toolkit.
[07:46] Tom Everett: timeline wise, if we start pilot next week what's realistic?
[07:50] Maya: if we get artifacts this week, we can stand up a hosted pilot in 3-4 business days and run a 10-day eval.
[07:58] Priya: one last Q — do you support customer-managed retention policies for transcripts and can we set redaction rules per route?
[08:05] Rajiv: yes, retention and redaction policies are per-route configurable, and we can enforce them in private deployments automatically.
[08:13] Maya: great. wrap-up: i'll send the pricing sheet and pilot plan, rajiv will send the security and private deployment architecture doc, dan will provide telemetry and prompts, priya will provide compliance checklist. we'll target the technical deep-dive next week.
[08:26] Lina: thanks all, this was useful.
[08:28] Tom Everett: thanks.
[08:30] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email.

Transcript notes: transcription imperfect in places (timestamps every ~30-80s), occasional speaker mislabels, filler words captured. references to "kv cache" and "vLLM" may be spelled differently in raw export.
